1. Restatement of Position  
   • My thesis: Coleman repeatedly manipulates Walker with false “Dream” tests and threats, provoking anxiety, sedation, and procedural caution, not genuine trust. Their “relationship” is that of trickster and wary victim, not blind compliance.  

2. Claim 1: Walker’s “probation” is procedural only; his sedation and reversals betray persistent doubt  
   a. Sedatives as evidence of distress  
      – “I took a pill and it went away. … I took two pills” (<quote> 19</quote>) each time Coleman’s “probation” offer appears. A man truly confident need not chemically calm himself.  
      – The only times Walker omits pills is when alone with Paulson/Horbit (whom he trusts enough to “explain” 4-D theory), not with Coleman. He “chewed up” performance pills only for his “job” (<quote> S</quote>), not for comfort with Coleman.  
   b. Reversals to protect career  
      – After first “Congratulations!” Walker “sat there and took it” (<quote> S</quote>) yet spends the day “if I got through… giving a good show” (<quote> S0</quote>), showing he must “perform” to earn release. If trust, no further “show.”  
      – Walker’s final decision vacillates “changed… then changed… back to… probation” (<quote> 1</quote>). Only a man fearing trickery would hedge rather than unconditionally free.  
   c. Threat of life sentence  
      – “I’m going to give you life in Dreamland” (<quote> 1</quote>) is Walker’s warning to Coleman if he “misuses” probation. Would a trusting warden threaten a committee superior with life imprisonment? This shows suspicion.  

3. Claim 2: Walker’s refusal to “wake” Coleman immediately and insistence on legal procedure  
   a. Invoking “the law” mechanically  
      – “That’s the law and you know it” (<quote> 19</quote>) when Keller objects to Coleman’s physical presence. Walker’s insistence on procedure is his only “safe” means of controlling Coleman’s power, not trust.  
      – With violent inmates, Walker “puts… to sleep” promptly (<quote>p. I m</quote>), but with Coleman he delays, “studies” him (<quote> S</quote>), and keeps him “distinguished” only because career sabotage is his only “weapon.” This is cautious containment, not hospitality.  
   b. Lack of evidence does not equal trust  
      – Walker’s own words: “I couldn’t afford to make a mistake” (<quote> S</quote>) when confronting the possibility this was a “jagged broadsword” test. If truly unsuspecting, he would have bet on release rather than “avoid tuning in tomorrow” (<quote> S0</quote>).  
      – “The only thing I knew was that I couldn’t tune in tomorrow and find out” (<quote> S1</quote>)—he prolongs limbo indefinitely due to fear of being wrong. A trusting mind would accept Coleman’s “test” and wake.  

4. Claim 3: Walker’s own admissions of ambivalence and desire for “proof”  
   a. Internal conflict reveals distrust  
      – “Did I want… probation… or… return to reality?” (<quote> S0</quote>) He debates staying in Dreamland rather than trusting Coleman’s promise. True belief would foreclose doubt.  
      – “It was a carousel… couldn’t catch the brass ring” (<quote> S2</quote>) suggests compulsion, not free acceptance, to continue the Dream just to test Coleman. He is trapped by doubt.  
   b. Gambit with Paulson and Horbit as proxies  
      – Walker “lied” to Paulson/Horbit (<quote> S3–17</quote>) to observe Coleman’s behavior indirectly. If Walker fully trusted Coleman’s assurances, he would have no need to create surrogate “tests.” He uses others as unwitting allies in his fight.  

5. Refutation of Debater_B Points  
   • B claims “repeated calm” and “granting favors” = trust. On the contrary:  
      – “Calm” accompanies “pills” and bureaucratic formality, a façade to mask anxiety.  
      – “Favors” are minimal: brief probation, no outright pardon, “if you misuse, I’ll give life.” This “favors” Coleman only as far as safe, not as a friend.  
   • B cites “act as if life real” resolve as moral test. But moral courage makes little sense unless Walker suspects trickery; blind faith requires no courage. His “courage” is fear-driven: afraid to be wrong about reality.  
   • B says no violence from Coleman. Coleman need not attack physically; his manipulations via career sabotage and false promises are subtler weapons. Walker recognizes this and shields himself with legal procedure and tests.  

6. Logical Coherence: Manipulator–Victim Model  
   • In every confrontation, Coleman wields institutional power and ambiguous information to provoke Walker’s worst fears: madness, career ruin, or permanent Dream.  
   • Walker, aware of his predecessors’ “loss of grip” (<quote> S</quote>), clings to procedure, sedatives, surrogate tests, and only minimal concessions.  
   • True believer would joyfully accept release and abandon the “nightmarish” role; Walker never does. His “reluctant” performance until the end—“Next visitor” (<quote>. co</quote>)—shows he expects further duping.  

Conclusion  
   The text consistently portrays Coleman as testing and tricking the warden, exploiting the machinery of Dreamland to manipulate him psychologically. Walker’s sedation, vacillation, legalistic caution, and auxiliary experiments with other “prisoners” manifest persistent distrust and distress. Therefore, the relationship is one of Coleman’s deception upsetting the warden, not naive compliance.
